title: Why big data systems exist, and when you don't need one
goal: By the end, you can say what a batch job is and why companies run them, estimate how long reading a pile of data takes, name the two ways to make it faster, and decide with arithmetic whether a job needs more than one computer.
opening:
Picture a jar of coins, filled a little every day for a year. On New Year's Eve, you tip it onto the table to count it. Nobody adds coins while you count, so the pile is complete before you start, and you go through it once.

It's a big pile, so you call three friends. Four people should take a quarter of the time. That's an easy guess, because it's how most chores feel. But someone has to split the heap and add up four totals, and the count isn't done until the slowest friend finishes.

In the last lesson, Streaming in Spark, the input never stopped arriving, and Spark (a program that runs one job on many computers) answered the same question for each new slice. This track starts from the other end: a pile complete before the work begins. In this lesson, we'll time one computer reading a big file of payments, split the reading over many machines and count the cost, then find a cheaper trick. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: A company that records card payments keeps a year of them in one file of 1 TB, a terabyte, which is a million megabytes (MB). The disk it sits on reads 500 MB a second. To total what each shop took, a program has to read the whole file once. About how long does the reading take?
options: It depends mostly on how cleverly the program is written
warmup.why: A million MB at 500 MB a second is 2,000 seconds, about 33 minutes. A total for every shop needs every payment, so the program has to read every byte, and no clever code makes the file smaller. Only two things shorten the wait: reading fewer bytes, or reading faster with more disks at once. This lesson builds both. The last option tempts anyone used to small files, where the code decides most of the speed. With a terabyte, the bytes do.

sections.h: Reading the whole pile once: what a batch job costs
sections.body:
People pay for coffee, books and groceries with a card, and a small company runs the program that records each payment: which card paid, which shop, how much and when. Every night, a program reads all of yesterday's payments, from first to last, and works out what to pay each shop.

That program is a **batch job**: a program that works through a large, fixed pile of input in one run and works out a result from all of it. The pile is complete before the job starts, like the coin jar. Nobody waits at a till for the answer, so the job can run at night, when the computers are quiet. And because it never changes its input, a job with a bug can be fixed and run again on the same pile.

Why read a huge pile in one go? Because some questions need everything. The company's accountants ask for one number per shop: how much it took last quarter. A program has to look at every payment in the quarter and add its amount to its shop's total. Every payment, once. Reading every record of a table, or of the part a question asks about, is called a **full scan**.

Here's one payment as a line of a CSV file. CSV means comma-separated values: a text file with one record per line and commas between the fields. You'll generate ten million made-up lines like it in a minute:

```text
0,2026-10-01 00:00:00,3352,FR,GBP,191136,AUTHORIZED,5037,0.3146,cfcd208495d565ef
```

Its ten fields are the payment's number, the time, the shop's number (`3352`), the card's country, the currency, the amount in cents (`191136` is 1,911.36), the status, and three more that the comparison box after the sections explains. The line is about 85 bytes, one byte per character, and ten million lines make an 846 MB file. A scan has to move all of it from the disk, through memory and through the processor. So its main cost is easy to write down:

```text
scan time = bytes read / bandwidth
```

**Bandwidth** is how many bytes per second one stage of that trip can move. The stages are the disk, sometimes a network link between computers, and the processor, which turns text into numbers. The slowest stage sets the speed of the whole trip, the way the narrowest pipe in a line of pipes sets the flow. Here are round numbers worth remembering. Disk makers count in thousands: 1 MB (megabyte) is 1,000,000 bytes, 1 GB (gigabyte) is 1,000 MB and 1 TB is 1,000,000 MB.

| Reader | Streams about | 1 TB takes |
|---|---|---|
| A hard disk | 200 MB/s | 83 minutes |
| A SATA SSD | 500 MB/s | 33 minutes |
| A laptop NVMe SSD | 3 GB/s | 6 minutes |
| A 10 Gb/s network link | 1.25 GB/s | 13 minutes |
| One processor core reading CSV | 0.7 GB/s (you'll measure it) | 24 minutes |

A hard disk keeps data on a spinning plate. An SSD (solid-state drive) has no moving parts; SATA is the older way to plug one in, NVMe the faster, newer way. A network link counts gigabits, and a byte is 8 bits, so 10 Gb/s moves 1.25 GB/s. A core is one of the processor's independent workers.

Most questions an app asks never meet this formula. To find one payment by its number, the payments program uses an index. An index is a lookup table from a key to where its record lives, like the index at the back of a book. That takes about a millisecond (a thousandth of a second), however big the file. But no index makes "every payment of the quarter" smaller. So the accountants' cost grows with the data: 846 MB takes a second or two, and 1 TB takes 33 minutes on a SATA SSD.

That growth is the problem big data systems were built for. Google, the search company, met it first, because its programs read stored copies of billions of web pages. Its 2004 paper on MapReduce, its system for jobs like these, mentions disks that read about 30 MB/s. At that speed one disk needs more than 9 hours to read 1 TB, and the paper says a typical job read many terabytes.

The figure below is the picture for the whole track: bytes to read, the readers that move them, and the time. There are only two ways to make the time smaller. Add readers, like the friends at the coin table (section 2), or shrink the bytes (section 3).

To measure the formula, you'll use DuckDB, a free program that answers questions about data files on one computer, from inside your own program. You ask it in SQL, the standard language for asking questions about tables of data, and each question is called a query. It reads CSV files, and also Parquet, a file format that stores a table column by column. Let's see how fast one core reads our file.

try.title: Time one core reading a CSV file
steps: From the `labs` folder, run the command below. The first run writes 10 million made-up payments to `bigdata/build/l01/`, once as CSV (846 MB) and once as Parquet (393 MB). That takes about 10 seconds, and later runs reuse the files. In the code, `SET threads = 1` tells DuckDB to use one core, like one reader.
Before you read the output, guess: does one core read the CSV faster or slower than a SATA SSD's 500 MB/s?
Read the speed it prints and its estimate for 1 TB. Run it twice more and see how much the number moves.

code.title: ScanDemo.kt
code.src:
package sfz.batch.l01.demo

/** Times one CPU core scanning a CSV file, then turns that speed into "how long for 1 TB". */
fun main() {
    PaymentFiles.open().use { c ->
        c.createStatement().use { it.execute("SET threads = 1") }        // one reader, like one disk
        val csv = PaymentFiles.csv
        val sql = "SELECT count(*), sum(amount_cents) FROM read_csv('${csv.absolutePath}')"
        val seconds = PaymentFiles.bestSeconds(c, sql)
        val bytesPerSecond = csv.length() / seconds
        println("file:      ${csv.name}, ${PaymentFiles.mb(csv.length())}, %,d rows".format(PaymentFiles.ROWS))
        println("one core:  %.2f s, so about %s per second".format(seconds, PaymentFiles.mb(bytesPerSecond.toLong())))
        println("1 TB at that speed: about %.0f minutes".format(1e12 / bytesPerSecond / 60))
    }
}

try.expect:
On a laptop with a 12-core Apple chip, it printed:

```text
file:      payments.csv, 846 MB, 10,000,000 rows
one core:  1.19 s, so about 713 MB per second
1 TB at that speed: about 23 minutes
```

Your speed will differ with your processor. The file was written seconds ago, so the operating system, the program that runs all the others, still holds it in memory. That copy is called the page cache, and while the file sits there the SSD barely works. The Operating systems track explains the page cache in The page cache, writeback and fsync. So what you measured is how fast one core splits CSV text into fields and turns them into numbers. Here the processor is the slowest stage, so it sets the bandwidth.

sections.h: More readers: split the pile across machines
sections.body:
Back at the coin table, calling friends is the obvious move, and it's the same with computers. If one disk needs 2,000 seconds for 1 TB, put half the file on a second disk, read both at once, and the scan takes 1,000 seconds. One computer holds only a few disks, so to go further you need more computers, which this track calls machines. A group of machines that work on one job together is a **cluster**. Spread the file over 100 machines, 10 GB each, and every machine reads its share in 20 seconds, all at the same time.

Growing by adding machines is called scale-out. The other choice, scale-up, means buying one bigger machine. In the early 2000s, a bigger machine cost far more and still had only a few disks, so Google built on racks (tall cabinets) full of cheap PCs. The MapReduce paper describes them: two processors, 2 to 4 GB of memory, cheap disks, and network links of 100 Mb/s or 1 Gb/s.

For the accountants' question, each machine works out a partial answer, the totals per shop for its own 10 GB. Then someone adds up the 100 partial answers. That someone is a **coordinator**, a program that cuts the work into pieces and starts one task on each machine. A task is one piece of work, here "scan this share and total it". The coordinator then combines the results, like you at the coin table, handing out heaps and adding up your friends' notes. Let's see what breaks on the way from one machine to a hundred. The stepper below walks through it with the same 1 TB file.

The first problem is starting up. The coordinator has to plan the job, start 100 tasks and collect 100 results, and that time doesn't shrink as you add machines. In the paper, a search for one pattern of text through 1 TB on about 1,800 machines took about 150 seconds, and about a minute of that was startup.

The second problem is the slowest machine. The job is done only when the last share is done. The paper describes a machine whose bad disk slowed its reads from 30 MB/s to 1 MB/s. One machine like that, called a **straggler**, holds up the other 99, like the friend who stops to admire every foreign coin.

The third is failure. On one machine, a dead disk is rare. With hundreds of cheap machines, says Google's paper on GFS, the Google File System, broken parts are the normal state of things. If a machine dies halfway, its share has to be read again elsewhere, so every share must exist on more than one machine. Lesson 3 of this track shows how Google kept those copies, and how Hadoop, a free rebuild of Google's design, keeps them too.

Splitting also has a floor. The coordinator hands out fixed-size pieces of a file, called blocks, not slivers of any size. In HDFS, Hadoop's file system for many machines, a block is 128 MiB. So it is in Spark, a free program that runs one job across many cores or machines. Most of this track uses Spark. MiB means binary megabytes, counted in powers of two: 128 times 1,048,576 is 134,217,728 bytes. 1 TB is 7,451 such blocks, so a 7,452nd machine has nothing to read. You'll work all of this out in the lab.

The coin table breaks as a picture in one place. Your friends sit in one room and can call out when they finish. Machines talk over a network, so every handout and every total is a message that takes time. And a machine that goes quiet may be slow, dead or cut off, and the coordinator can't tell which. Next, we'll pull the other lever and read fewer bytes.

frames.say: Machine 2 has a failing disk and reads at a tenth of the speed. Its share takes 200 seconds, and the job can't finish without it. **The slowest machine sets the time.** With a thousand machines, one is always slow or broken, so the system has to notice and run that share again somewhere else.

try.title: Add readers on your laptop
steps: Run `ThreadsDemo` with the command below. It runs the same CSV scan with DuckDB allowed 1, 2, 4 and 8 threads, then all your cores. A thread is one line of work inside a program, and each one can run on its own core. Here each thread scans its own chunks of the file, the way machines scan their own blocks.
Predict first: with 8 threads, is it 8 times faster than with 1?
Compare the speedup column with the number of cores your computer has.

code.title: ThreadsDemo.kt

try.expect:
On the same 12-core laptop:

```text
 1 threads: 1.18 s   speedup 1.0x
 2 threads: 0.63 s   speedup 1.9x
 4 threads: 0.34 s   speedup 3.4x
 8 threads: 0.20 s   speedup 5.8x
12 threads: 0.18 s   speedup 6.4x
```

The speedup grows, but more slowly than the thread count. DuckDB still has to split the file and add up the partial sums at the end. Many laptop chips mix fast and slow cores. And every thread shares one path to memory. A cluster flattens out the same way, with the network between machines in place of that shared path.

aside.title: Why not buy one bigger machine instead?
aside.body: Often you can, and it goes much further than in Google's early days. AWS, Amazon's business that rents out computers over the internet, has rented out one machine since December 2024 with 1,920 vCPUs and 32 TiB of memory. (A vCPU is one rented thread's worth of processor.) Jordan Tigani, whom section 4 introduces, notes that a standard rented machine grew from 1 core and 2 GB of memory in 2006 to 64 cores and 256 GB. The catches are price, since the biggest machines cost more per core, and the few disks one machine can read from. And if it breaks, the whole job stops with it. Growing past one machine, in the Foundations track, weighs the two choices in detail.

sections.h: Fewer bytes: store the payments column by column
sections.body:
Look at the CSV line again. The accountants need two of its ten fields: the shop (`3352`) and the amount (`191136`). The scan still reads all 85 bytes. In a CSV file the fields of one payment sit next to each other, and the next payment starts only after the last field of this one. So the reader can't jump from one amount to the next. It has to walk through every byte of every line. Storing each record's values together like this is a **row layout**.

The coin jar has the same problem. Its coins are all mixed together, so to count the 2-euro coins you pick through every coin in the heap. If the coins had gone into tubes, one tube for each kind, you'd pick up one tube and leave the rest.

That's the fix for the file, too: store the table the other way round. All payment numbers first, then all the times, then all the shops, and so on. (The comparison box after the sections shows three payments both ways.) Now a question that needs two columns reads two runs of values and skips the other eight. Storing each column's values together is a **columnar layout**. The Storage engines track built one inside a database, in Column stores and compression. Parquet, the format most of this track uses, is the same idea as a file that almost any data tool can read.

Columns also compress well, which means they fit in fewer bytes, because the values in one column look alike. The `currency` column in our data holds only four different values. Instead of writing `EUR` ten million times, a file can keep the list `EUR, USD, GBP, INR` once and store a tiny number per payment that points into it. The `status` column works the same way. Lesson 5 of this track, Columnar files, shows the tricks Parquet uses.

The third way to read less is to skip data that can't match. If the payments are stored in one folder per day, a question about last week opens seven folders and ignores the rest (lesson 4). If each file notes the earliest and latest time inside it, a reader can skip every file whose times can't match (lesson 5).

Here the coin picture stops working. You can see at a glance which tube holds what, but a program can't see inside a file. The file has to be built by column, with notes about what's inside, on purpose. Otherwise the program must read everything to find out.

Put the three together on the 1 TB file. Say it has 30 columns and the accountants need 3, which make up a tenth of each row. Stored by column, the question reads 100 GB. If those columns compress 5 times, it reads 20 GB. At 500 MB/s that's 40 seconds on one machine. On a laptop's NVMe SSD at 3 GB/s, it's about 7 seconds.

| Plan | Bytes read | Time |
|---|---|---|
| One machine, row layout | 1 TB | 2,000 s |
| 100 machines, row layout | 10 GB each | 20 s plus startup |
| One machine, columns, compressed | 20 GB | 40 s (7 s on NVMe) |

Against SATA SSDs, the hundred machines still win on paper, 20 seconds to 40. Against a laptop's NVMe SSD, they lose. And they cost a hundred machines, while the columnar plan costs a file format. **Shrink the bytes first, then decide whether you need more readers.** Every engine in this track, Spark included, works hard to read less before it reads faster. (An engine is a program that runs questions over data.) So how often does a company need the hundred machines at all? Next, we'll look at real numbers.

try.title: Count the bytes each format reads
steps: Run `FewerBytesDemo`. It asks one question of the CSV file: count the payments and add up `amount_cents`. Then it reads all ten columns of the Parquet file, and asks the first question of the Parquet file. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` makes DuckDB run each query and report what it did, including how many bytes it read.
Predict the bytes read for each line before you look. Does the CSV query read only two columns' worth?
Compare the `read` column with the file sizes on the first line.

code.title: FewerBytesDemo.kt

try.expect:
```text
files: csv 846 MB, parquet 393 MB
csv, 2 columns      read 988.2 MB in 0.194s
parquet, all 10     read 390.7 MB in 0.120s
parquet, 2 columns  read 47.7 MB in 0.0089s
```

The CSV query reads the whole file, and DuckDB even counts a little more than its size. The question needs only the amounts, but in a row layout the other fields sit between them, so the reader has to go through those too. Parquet with all ten columns reads about its file size. The two-column Parquet query reads 48 MB, about 5% of the CSV. DuckDB answers `count(*)` from the row counts Parquet stores inside the file, and reads only the compressed `amount_cents` column. The times are tiny because both files sit in the page cache, the operating system's copy of recently read files in memory. From a disk that hasn't read the files yet, or from storage across a network such as Amazon S3, the bytes decide the time.

sections.h: How big is big? Most data fits on one machine
sections.body:
So how big is "big"? Growing past one machine, in the Foundations track, made the general case with the COST paper, a 2015 study of published systems. A cluster first has to beat one well-written program that runs on a single thread, one line of work, on the same problem. The systems the paper looked at often needed hundreds of cores to do that, or never managed it. Here's the same question in this lesson's terms.

Jordan Tigani was a founding engineer on BigQuery, Google's paid service that runs SQL over very large tables on Google's own computers. In his 2023 post "Big Data is Dead", he looked at how customers really used it. Most had less than 1 TB of data in total. Among customers who spent more than $1,000 a year, 90% of queries read less than 100 MB. His figures come from one product, and he calls them approximate. Our payments company fits the pattern: it might keep a few hundred GB of payments, and most questions people ask read last week's slice.

Put his numbers into this lesson's formula. At the 0.7 GB/s at which one core reads CSV, 100 MB takes about a seventh of a second. Even the 1 TB file from section 3, read as 3 compressed columns out of 30, is 20 GB: under 10 seconds on one NVMe disk. For most questions most companies ask, one machine is enough.

So when do you need a cluster? When the bytes a job must read, after skipping everything it can, are more than one machine can scan in the time you have. That happens when several terabytes of new data arrive every day. It happens with a backfill, a job that works out results again over years of past payments, say after a bug fix. It happens when a job joins two huge tables, matching each record in one with its partners in the other. And it happens when you prepare years of payments to train a fraud model, a program that learns from old payments to spot suspicious new ones. You also need a cluster when a job runs for hours and must survive a machine failing halfway, or when many teams share one copy of the data.

Spark exists for those cases. Even Spark agrees about the rest: Spark 4.3 added an opt-in setting, `spark.sql.optimizer.singleTaskExecution.enabled`, that runs small queries as a single task instead of spreading them over the cluster.

The formula has a limit, too. It prices the reading and nothing else. Totals per shop are cheap once the bytes arrive, because there are only a few thousand shops. Ask how many payments each card made, and there are millions of cards. Bringing each card's payments together then costs memory and sorting, and on a cluster it means sending data between machines. That's often the slow part of a real job.

The track follows that thread. Lesson 2 runs a whole batch job on one machine and shows the two ways any engine brings matching records together: a table in memory, or sorting. Lessons 3 to 8 spread the job over many machines, from Google's MapReduce to the way Spark runs, moves and plans a job. Lessons 9 to 12 cover Spark 4 from Java and Kotlin, databases built for analysis, and tables kept as files in cheap storage. The last three cover running many jobs in the right order, what batch output is for, and choosing an engine. DuckDB on one machine stays a real option every time.

refs.title: Big Data is Dead (Jordan Tigani, MotherDuck)
Scalability! But at what COST? (McSherry, Isard and Murray, HotOS 2015)

compare.title: The same three payments, by row and by column

b.label: Column layout (Parquet, simplified)
b.title: payments.parquet
b.src:
payment_id       0 | 1 | 2
created_at       2026-10-01 00:00:00 | 2026-10-17 08:52:32 | 2026-10-08 21:40:34
merchant_id      3352 | 3834 | 3982
card_country     FR | BR | US
currency         GBP | EUR | EUR
amount_cents     191136 | 170792 | 178237
status           AUTHORIZED | CAPTURED | DECLINED
mcc              5037 | 5446 | 5369
fraud_score      0.3146 | 0.5569 | 0.7361
idempotency_key  cfcd208495d565ef | c4ca4238a0b92382 | c81e728d9d4c2f63

compare.note: Both hold the same three payments from the demo files. The first seven fields are the payment's number, its time, the shop's number, the card's country, the currency, the amount in cents and the status. `AUTHORIZED` means the card's bank set the money aside, `CAPTURED` that the money really moved, and `DECLINED` that the bank said no. Then comes a four-digit code for the kind of shop (`mcc`, merchant category code; made up here). Next is a fraud score from 0 to 1 that a fraud model gave the payment. Last is an idempotency key, a unique label the app sends with each request so that a retried request isn't recorded twice. To add up `amount_cents` from the CSV, the reader goes through every line and splits out the sixth field. In the column layout, all the amounts sit together, so the reader fetches that one run of values and skips the other nine. Values in a column also look alike (the same few currencies, statuses from a short list), which is why columns compress so well. Real Parquet first cuts the rows into chunks called row groups and stores each chunk column by column. At the end of the file, in the footer, it keeps an index of where every column starts. Lesson 5 opens one up.

worked.title: Size a big recount before you rent a cluster

steps.say: A fraud analyst, someone whose job is spotting suspicious payments, wants one number worked out again for every payment of the last 18 months. The number is how many payments the same card made in the hour before. That's about 2.2 billion payments, kept in the company's database at roughly 200 bytes each. First, describe the data as it sits today. The job needs four columns; lump the rest together.
Next, work out the bytes the job reads, stored as rows and stored as compressed columns. Assume Parquet makes these four columns 4 times smaller; lesson 5 checks real ratios.
steps.code:
// 2. bytes read: the row store drags all 200 bytes along
val need = setOf("card_id", "merchant_id", "amount_cents", "created_at")
val rowBytes = ScanMath.bytesRead(asRows, need)                         // 440 GB
val asParquet = asRows.copy(layout = Layout.COLUMNAR, compressionRatio = 4.0)
val columnBytes = ScanMath.bytesRead(asParquet, need)                   // 15.4 GB

steps.say: Then time both plans on hardware you could rent. One is a machine with a 3 GB/s NVMe disk. The other is a cluster of 20 machines with 500 MB/s SATA SSDs and 30 seconds of startup.

Decide. The single machine wins by more than ten times, because it reads 28 times fewer bytes. The expensive step is copying the 440 GB out of the database into Parquet files. Do that once, keep the files, and run every later recount against them.

lab.title: Build a scan calculator for quick estimates
steps: From the `labs` folder, run the tests once with the command above. Tests are small programs that check your code and say what's wrong. All nine fail with `NotImplementedError` for now. The first run downloads Spark and DuckDB for the whole track, so give it a minute.
Write `scanSeconds` and `blockCount`. Keep `blockCount` in `Long` arithmetic, whole numbers that go up to about 9 billion billion: one test feeds it 10 PB (ten petabytes, 10,000 TB) in 1-byte blocks.
Write `clusterSeconds`. The busiest machine gets `ceil(blocks / machines)` blocks, the division rounded up, but never more bytes than the file has. Startup is added once.
Write `bytesRead`. A `ROW` table reads every column, whatever the query needs. Reject unknown columns first.
Write `machinesNeeded` with a plain loop over machine counts. Return `null` when even one block per machine is too slow.
Run the tests until all nine pass. Then read the test names from top to bottom: together they make this lesson's argument.
hints: To divide whole numbers and round up, use `(a + b - 1) / b`. It stays exact for any `Long` this lab uses.
In `bytesRead`, multiply before you divide: `Math.round(rows.toDouble() * bytesPerRow / compressionRatio)`.
More machines than blocks can't help, so the loop in `machinesNeeded` can stop at `blockCount(bytes, blockSize)`.

drill.title: Estimate a cluster scan from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. A 5 TB file of payment records sits as CSV on 40 machines with 200 MB/s disks, in 128 MiB blocks, and the job has 45 seconds of startup. On paper, how long does a full scan take? Then write `clusterSeconds` from memory and check your number with it.

recap: A batch job reads a large, fixed pile of input in one run and works out its result from all of it. It runs when nobody is waiting, and a bad run can be fixed and run again on the same pile.
A full scan costs the bytes read divided by the bandwidth of the slowest stage: the disk, the network or the processor turning text into numbers. 1 TB at 500 MB/s is 2,000 seconds.

Splitting the bytes across machines (scale-out) adds startup, waits for the slowest machine and has to survive failures. It also stops at the number of blocks: 1 TB in 128 MiB blocks is at most 7,451 tasks.
Reading fewer bytes (columns, compression, skipping files that can't match) is the cheaper lever. Pull it before you add machines.
Most companies' data, and most of the questions they ask, fit on one machine. Do the arithmetic before you reach for Spark.

The limit: the formula prices only the reading. Bringing each card's or shop's records together costs memory, sorting and, on a cluster, traffic between machines, and that's often the slow part of a real job.
closing:
We started with a jar of coins and three friends. More helpers cost startup, wait for the slowest and can quit halfway, while coins sorted into tubes beat them all. Data works the same way: read fewer bytes first, then decide whether you need more readers.

On a Mac or Linux, try the formula on a big file of your own, such as a video: `time cat video.mp4 > /dev/null`. Its size divided by the first run's seconds is your disk's bandwidth. Run it again, and the page cache makes it faster.

Next, we'll run a whole batch job on one machine with five small programs, and find out how a computer counts things that don't fit in its memory.

quiz.q: A nightly job reads 600 GB of Parquet files from object storage, a storage service on other machines that you reach over the network, such as Amazon S3. The machine running the job pulls 1.5 GB/s from that storage, and its processor decodes Parquet at 4 GB/s. Roughly how long does the scan take?
quiz.why: The slowest stage sets the bandwidth, and here that's the storage: 600 GB at 1.5 GB/s is 400 seconds, about 7 minutes. The tempting 2.5 minutes uses the decoding speed, but the processor can only decode bytes that have arrived.

quiz.q: A 2 GB file is stored in 128 MiB blocks, and the scan runs one task per block. You run it on a cluster of 50 idle machines. How many machines do any work?
quiz.why: 2,000,000,000 / 134,217,728 = 14.9, so the file has 15 blocks and the scan has 15 tasks. The other 35 machines wait. The tempting 16 comes from dividing by 128,000,000 instead of 128 MiB, and 50 assumes the work splits as finely as you like.

quiz.q: A table has 40 columns of about the same width. A question needs 4 of them. You move the table from CSV to a columnar format that makes it 4 times smaller. Roughly how many fewer bytes does the question read?
options: No change, because a question reads whole rows either way
quiz.why: Reading 4 of 40 columns cuts the bytes 10 times, and compression cuts them 4 times more: 40 times fewer. "10 times" forgets compression. A columnar format exists so that a question doesn't read whole rows.

quiz.q: You double the machines on a scan job, and the run time barely changes. Which explanation fits best?
options: Startup, or one slow machine, already took most of the time
The files are in a columnar format
Each machine now reads fewer blocks
quiz.why: Doubling the machines halves only the part of the job that splits: the reading. Startup is paid once, and the job waits for its slowest machine, so if those take most of the time, more machines don't help. Fewer blocks per machine is what should have made it faster; the reading just wasn't what held the job back.

quiz.q: A team stores 300 GB of payment records. People ask questions about the last 7 days, about 6 GB, a few times an hour. What should the team try first?
options: A 20-machine Spark cluster, so questions stay fast as the data grows
Keep the CSV files and buy a machine with more cores
Load everything into Kafka, a program that keeps long logs of messages, and keep it for years
Store it in one folder per day in a columnar format, and ask a one-machine engine such as DuckDB
quiz.why: The questions read about 6 GB, and less after skipping columns and compressing. One machine scans that in seconds. A cluster adds startup, cost and machines to look after, for a problem that isn't there yet. More cores help CSV a little, but reading fewer bytes helps far more. Kafka hands messages to programs in order; it isn't built to answer questions about them.

flashcards.back: A program that works through a large, fixed pile of input in one run and works out a result from all of it, usually on a schedule. Its input doesn't change, so a bad run can be fixed and run again.

flashcards.front: What's your first estimate for a full scan's time?
flashcards.back: Bytes read divided by the bandwidth of the slowest stage (the disk, the network or the processor decoding the file). 1 TB at 500 MB/s is 2,000 s.

flashcards.front: Why can't 10,000 machines scan a 1 TB file in 128 MiB blocks faster than 7,451 machines can?
flashcards.back: Work comes in blocks, one task each. 1 TB is 7,451 blocks, so the extra machines have nothing to read.

flashcards.front: What does scale-out cost besides the extra machines?
flashcards.back: Startup and coordination that don't shrink, waiting for the slowest machine, and running work again when a machine fails.

flashcards.front: A question needs 3 of 30 equally wide columns, and the format compresses them 5 times. What fraction of a 1 TB row scan does it read?
Why is the second run of a scan on your laptop often much faster than the first?
flashcards.back: The operating system keeps the file in memory, in its page cache, so the second run reads memory instead of the disk.

flashcards.front: What did Tigani report about BigQuery query sizes?
flashcards.back: Most customers had less than 1 TB in total, and among customers spending over $1,000 a year, 90% of queries read less than 100 MB.

terms.plain: A program that reads a large, fixed pile of input in one run and works out its result from all of it.
Reading every record of a table, or of the part a question needs.
How many bytes per second a stage can move: a disk, a network link, or a processor decoding a file.
Making one machine bigger: more cores, memory and disks.
Adding machines and splitting the work between them.
The slowest machine or task in a job split over many. The job can't finish before it does.
Storing each column's values together, so a question reads only the columns it names.
Memory where the operating system keeps recently read file data, so the next read skips the disk.

explain_back.prompt: A manager at the payments company asks whether the team needs a Spark cluster for a new store of reports. It holds 2 TB today and grows 50 GB a month, and its screens show the last 30 days. Answer with numbers.
explain_back.answer: Not yet. The size that matters is what the screens read, not what we store. Thirty days is about 50 GB at today's rate. Stored by column and in one folder per day, a screen that needs 5 of 40 columns reads about an eighth of that, roughly 6 GB. If the columns compress 4 times, that's about 1.5 GB. One machine with an NVMe disk reads that in under a second. A cluster would add startup time, wait for its slowest machine and need looking after, and it would buy us nothing at this size. I'd look again if one question had to read many terabytes, or if jobs ran for hours and had to survive a machine failing.

deeper.body:
**Why a minute of startup mattered so much.** The part of a job that doesn't split puts a ceiling on how much faster more machines can make it. This is Amdahl's law, named after the computer designer Gene Amdahl, and the scan formula makes it concrete.

Take the 1 TB scan at 500 MB/s with 60 seconds of fixed startup. On one machine it takes 60 + 2,000 = 2,060 seconds. On *n* machines it takes 60 + 2,000 / *n*. However large *n* gets, it never drops below 60 seconds, so the speedup can never beat 2,060 / 60, about 34 times. With 100 machines you already get 2,060 / 80, about 26 times. The other 1,700 machines buy the last few times.

**Reading from object storage.** Amazon S3 and services like it keep files as named objects. You fetch them over HTTP, the same rules a web browser uses to fetch a page. Reading a file from S3 is a series of requests, and each one waits tens of milliseconds before its first byte arrives. One request at a time reads slowly, so engines ask for many pieces of a file at once and keep many requests in flight. That's why DuckDB 2.0 added asynchronous reading for Parquet and CSV files aimed at object storage: it sends the next requests without waiting for the last ones to come back. The formula still holds. The bandwidth just depends on how many requests you keep busy.

**Two ways to fool yourself.** The first is sizing a job by the size of the table instead of the bytes the question reads. A team hears "the payments table is 4 TB" and asks for a cluster. But the table covers three years, and the reports read 4 of its 60 columns for the last 30 days: about 7 GB before compression. The second is timing a query twice on a laptop, getting the fast second run from the page cache, and assuming the real storage reads that fast. Both have the same fix. Write down the bytes read after skipping columns and folders, take the bandwidth of the slowest stage on the real hardware, and divide.
